When Mary Shelley died in 1851, her Frankenstein had already become a classic.
The novel, which some see as a simple horror story and others acclaim as one of the first works of science fiction, continues to inspire writers and filmmakers around the world.
Whether in the modern literary genre of science fiction or in a Hollywood monster movie, the tale of Mary Shelley’s monster lives on as one of the most recognizable narratives in English literature.

episodes.title: Martin Luther King Jr.

subtitle.text: One of the greatest public speakers of the twentieth century, civil-rights leader Martin Luther King Jr. was
born on January 15, 1929, during a turbulent period in American history. Although slavery had been abolished
many decades earlier, African Americans in the South were still subject to a series of unjust laws
that forbid them from voting and made it impossible to completely integrate into mainstream society. They were required
to attend segregated—and usually inferior—schools, use separate public facilities (such as washrooms, drinking fountains, and swimming pools),
and generally defer to whites in most aspects of daily life. Many blacks were growing increasingly frustrated
and resentful of the inequality, poverty, and lack of freedom in their homeland. When Martin Luther King
Jr. rose to the challenge and spoke out in support of civil rights for all Americans, the
people and their politicians listened. Through his powerful speeches and peaceful actions, he helped transform American culture
and forced many Americans to examine their racist attitudes. Raised in a middle-class family in Atlanta, Georgia, King
was unaware of the prejudices that faced African Americans until a white playmate told him that they
could no longer be friends because his parents didn’t want him playing with a black child. This
early experience shaped King’s beliefs and spurred him to try to create a more nurturing world, one
in which his children would not have to face racial discrimination as they grew up. As a
young man, King earned a degree in theology and became a Baptist pastor in Montgomery, Alabama. There,
he encouraged members of his church to stand up for themselves and reject the inequality perpetuated through
racial segregation. At the same time, as a scholar who had studied the life and works of Indian
pacifist Mohandas Gandhi, King discouraged violence in any form, firmly believing that equality would arise out of
peaceful actions. The momentum for civil rights grew gradually until a single event in Montgomery captured the
attention of Americans across the country. On December 1, 1955, a black woman named Rosa Parks was
arrested for refusing to give up her seat on the bus to a white passenger. This brave
act triggered a watershed; huge numbers of protests took place, and within days, a group of civil-rights
advocates organized a challenge to racial segregation laws. King was asked to lead a boycott of the Montgomery
public transportation system, and he accepted. In his 1958 memoir of the boycott, Stride Toward Freedom ,
he wrote, "We came to see that, in the long run, it is more honorable to walk
in dignity than ride in humiliation. So . . . we decided to substitute tired feet for
tired souls, and walk the streets of Montgomery." Starting on December 5, more than 90 percent of
Montgomery’s black citizens walked, bicycled, or even rode mules to work instead of taking the bus. Some
whites supported the boycott by driving their black maids to and from work. Cab drivers also supported
the boycott by taking black passengers for the ten-cent bus fare. Even though his home was firebombed and
he was arrested, King continued to lead the boycott for over a year. Their work came to
fruition in 1956, when the United States Supreme Court ruled that segregated buses were unconstitutional and forced
the city to desegregate its buses. After this success, King helped establish the Southern Christian Leadership Conference
(SCLC), an organization that would mobilize people all over the country to fight for justice and equal
opportunities for African Americans. The SCLC provided King with plenty of opportunities to give lectures around the
country, speaking at church functions and political events. He met with other civil-rights leaders and international advocates for
equality, looking frequently to activists in South Africa and India for guidance and support. As president of
the SCLC, King participated in hundreds of nonviolent protests against social injustice. At one such event in
1960, King was arrested and sentenced to prison, but Democratic presidential candidate John F. Kennedy arranged for
his release. Kennedy’s support of King during this highly publicized event proved to be key in Kennedy’s
election a few weeks later. The height of King’s prominence occurred during the early 1960s. King and
several other civil-rights leaders organized the historic March on Washington, an assembly of about 250,000 people of
many races. On August 28, 1963, the group gathered in peaceful protest around the Lincoln Memorial to demand
the equal treatment of all citizens. It was during this event that King inspired the crowd with
his famous "I have a dream" speech, in which he said, "I have a dream that my
four little children will one day live in a nation where they will not be judged by
the color of their skin but by the content of their character." As King had hoped, the
momentous march helped bring about the adoption of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which required nationwide
desegregation and outlawed racial discrimination. That December, King was awarded the Nobel Prize for Peace. At 35, he
was one of its youngest recipients. With characteristic humility and grace, King turned his prize money over
to the civil-rights movement. But some African Americans, especially in poor urban neighborhoods, were growing impatient with
King’s nonviolent protests and the slow pace of change. The more aggressive, often violent, tactics advocated by
radical activists such as Malcolm X were gathering supporters. They believed that only a revolution would allow
African Americans to reach their goals. A series of riots in the latter half of the 1960s
marked the beginning of the "black power" movement. This type of activism challenged King’s less confrontational approach
and created a growing divide between groups like the SCLC, which wanted to work peacefully for social change,
and those that asserted that the time for negotiation had passed. In spite of the increasing tension,
King continued to work for change without violence and invited people from all socioeconomic groups and all
racial backgrounds to join in his struggle. King’s efforts to unite whites and blacks in a common
desire for equality, however, were interrupted on April 4, 1968, when he was shot and killed as
he stood on the second-story balcony of a hotel in Memphis, Tennessee. The assassin, a white man
named James Earl Ray, was caught two months later and sentenced to 99 years in prison. A man
of deep convictions, a talented speaker, and a natural leader, Martin Luther King Jr. was one of
the most influential voices in American history. He was only 39 years old when he died, but
his legacy is still visible in contemporary society, most importantly in the modern-day struggle for social justice.

episodes.title: John F. Kennedy: An American Icon

subtitle.text: The name Kennedy has become synonymous in the United States with wealth, power, and tragedy. John Fitzgerald Kennedy, the
35th president of the United States, personified all of these. He led his country into a new era, one
of aggressive Cold War maneuvers and mass media politics. He was a new breed of politician, one who came
from a wealthy background but stood up for the rights of minorities. Although his presidency was tragically short—less
than three years—his legacy has endured. John F. Kennedy was born the second child of Joseph and Rose Kennedy.
Joe, an Irish American multimillionaire, had a burning ambition for his sons to run for political office. He encouraged
his nine children to be competitive in both their physical and intellectual pursuits. The combination of financial independence and
competitiveness was a major factor in the Kennedy family’s political success. After the oldest son, Joe Jr., was killed
in World War II, John Kennedy took up the family’s ambitions. He had already served in World War II,
been injured, returned to battle, and shown exceptional bravery—for which he was awarded the U.S. Navy and Marine
Corps Medal for heroism. Because of his injuries, he continued to suffer back pain for the rest of his
life. Nevertheless, soon after he was discharged from the navy in 1945, Kennedy began to run a very aggressive
campaign for a seat in the U.S. House of Representatives. At the age of 29, he won his first
election. He never lost an election throughout his political career. In 1952 he ran for the U.S. Senate, with
his brother Robert managing the campaign. The following year he married the young, beautiful, and sophisticated Jacqueline Lee Bouvier,
whose prominent family enhanced his social position. In the following years, he and his wife appeared on many
magazine covers, in newspapers, and on television broadcasts as he delivered speeches and made public appearances. The couple’s glamour
was very important in the emerging age of television. In January 1960 John F. Kennedy formally announced his intention
to run for president of the United States. He launched a new kind of political campaign, using the mass
media to advertise himself. The Kennedy style—intellectual, classy, and rich—captivated the hearts and minds of Americans. Kennedy’s charm, wit,
and eloquence——teamed with Jacqueline’s artistic sense and fine taste—fascinated the media and the adoring American public. Everything the Kennedys
did, wore, ate, and said became fashionable. Largely due to Kennedy’s popularity with the public, the Democratic Party
nominated him as their candidate. One of the deciding factors in the presidential campaign was a series of televised
debates between the two candidates. With his handsome face, distinctly Harvard accent, and poise in front of the cameras,
Kennedy eclipsed his less charismatic opponent, Richard M. Nixon. It is estimated that 85 to 120 million Americans watched
one or more of the debates, and most viewers concluded that Kennedy had won them, even though both candidates
showed a clear grasp of the issues and were equally articulate in expressing their views. Since then every president
elected to the Oval Office has had to prove his adeptness with the media, especially television. John F.
Kennedy’s presidential campaign slogan, "Let’s get this country moving again," applied to both international and domestic affairs. On an
international level, he vowed to involve America more in world matters. He wanted to build missiles to catch up
to a perceived Soviet dominance, as well as to defend the U.S. from communist Cuba. Domestically he pledged to
raise employment, improve the economy, and support civil rights. Kennedy won the election—the youngest president ever elected to the
White House. In his inaugural speech, he stirred the hearts of Americans when he said, "In the long history
of the world, only a few generations have been granted the role of defending freedom in its hour
of maximum danger. I do not shrink from this responsibility—I welcome it." He concluded with these immortal words, "My
fellow Americans: ask not what your country can do for you—ask what you can do for your country." Soon
after he became president, the Cold War escalated into a crisis. In October 1962 the world held its breath
as tensions between the U.S. and the Soviet Union came to a head. The Soviets had begun to install
nuclear missiles on Cuba, an island only 145 kilometers away from the American state of Florida. On October 24
Kennedy ordered a naval blockade to stop Soviet ships from reaching Cuba. For 13 long days, the two
nations were on the brink of nuclear war. On October 28 the Soviet leader, Nikita Khrushchev, backed down. He
promised that no more missiles would be delivered to Cuba and that the ones already on the island would
be removed. In return Kennedy promised not to invade Cuba. The rivalry between the superpowers did not end there.
The Cold War resulted in American involvement in the Vietnam War, a step seen as critical to preventing the
spread of communism. According to the "domino theory," if one small country were to fall to the communists,
many more in the region would follow. As a result Kennedy promised financial and military aid to the South
Vietnamese, who were battling the communist North Vietnamese, and sent thousands of American soldiers there to fight. After 15
years of bitter conflict that left thousands of Americans and Vietnamese dead and wounded, American soldiers withdrew, defeated, and
Vietnam became a communist state. Within the borders of the United States, however, Kennedy left three lasting legacies: the
space program, the Peace Corps, and the Civil Rights Act. After the Soviets’ success in launching the world’s first
satellite into orbit in 1957, Kennedy ordered American scientists at NASA to put an American man on the moon
by the end of the 1960s. This resulted in a huge expansion of the American space program, which
did reach its goal in July 1969. The Peace Corps is a government agency that sends American volunteers to
developing countries in order to improve American relations with other nations. The Civil Rights Act proposed by Kennedy made
racial discrimination in public places illegal, and made it possible to withhold federal government aid from states that continued
to practice segregation. This led to the Voting Rights Act in 1965, which protected the rights of blacks to
vote in elections and allowed the emergence of many African American political leaders. Tragically on November 22, 1963, as
John and Jacqueline Kennedy were riding in an open motorcade in Dallas, Texas, the president was shot and
killed. Just two hours later, Vice President Lyndon Johnson was sworn in as the new president. Although a loner
named Lee Harvey Oswald was arrested almost immediately and charged with the assassination, he was himself killed just two
days later, before he could come to trial. Conspiracy theories about who was responsible for the JFK assassination are
plentiful. Speculation about mafia or CIA involvement has flourished in books, movies, and magazines over the past forty years.
JFK’s presidency has been described as "one brief shining moment" in history, and the man himself is a cultural
and political icon; decades after his death, his popularity has not diminished. Sadly, in 1968, JFK’s brother Robert
was also assassinated, during his bid to become president. The successes and tragedies that befell the Kennedy clan have
been immortalized in countless books, movies, and even Broadway plays. Generations after, the world still remembers John F. Kennedy.

episodes.title: The Rise of the Roman Empire

subtitle.text: Historical accounts of ancient Rome paint the civilization as a fierce society that achieved incredible feats of architecture and engineering and developed complex systems of law and government.
Yet, in 753 BC, the legendary date of the founding of Rome, the city was nothing more than a marketplace for several tribes from the nearby hillsides.
But its strategic location on the Italian peninsula, on the banks of the Tiber River, allowed it to rapidly grow into a thriving metropolis.
At its peak, Rome was the center of a vast empire, spanning the Mediterranean from western Europe all the way to northern Africa.
Roman history is usually divided into three main periods.
From its foundation until the sixth century BC, the political landscape was dominated by a succession of kings.
This stage, however, was short-lived because the monarchy was overthrown and replaced by a republican government in 509 BC.
The Roman Republic, recognized as the second period, was controlled by the Senate, a legislative arm of government made up of male citizens from aristocratic families, who were senators for life.
Women and poor men were not eligible to join at all.
The Senate was responsible for advising two leaders, called "consuls," who controlled the army, set taxes, and executed the laws.
Both consuls had to agree on all decisions; if one of them vetoed a proposed law, then it would not go into force.
This sharing of power, coupled with the presence of the Senate, ensured that no single person controlled the entire republic.
This approach, involving a balance of powers, has become the basis of many contemporary governments, including that of the United States.
In addition to senators, there were prefects, officials who took care of such routine matters as running the market and the fire brigade, and a tribune, whose job was to speak for the poor people.
The tribune also had the ability to veto some decisions, but rarely invoked this power because his position was primarily symbolic.
Finally, there was the Assembly, composed entirely of adult men.

The Assembly nominated consuls, prefects, and senators, as well as the tribune, but these elections were controlled by the wealthy classes, who usually selected members of their own families for these positions.
A series of military victories, however, ushered in the third and final period of ancient Roman history: the Roman Empire.
The Romans had begun to conquer distant territories, which necessitated the development of new government positions to manage matters in those foreign lands.
Many seats in the Assembly were left empty, because the soldiers who had occupied them were away on the battlefields.
As a result of their armies' support, generals became more influential.
By around 50 BC, these leaders had become so powerful that they no longer listened to the commands of consuls and ignored the recommendations of the Senate.
This allowed the general Julius Caesar to become dictator of the Roman Republic, laying the foundations of the Roman Empire.
After Julius Caesar was murdered by his own statesmen, another clever general, Augustus Caesar, rose to power.
He realized that he could reorganize the government to keep the Senate and consuls, which appeased the Assembly, but give himself supreme authority.
His restructuring made him the first emperor of the Roman Empire in 27 BC.
By the end of his reign, Augustus had brought many hostile territories under control of the Roman legions.
This feat ushered in a two-hundred-year period of peace and prosperity, marred by only a few ongoing frontier conflicts.
During the Pax Romana (Roman Peace), as the period was known, literature, science, and the arts flourished throughout the empire.
Doctors began to study anatomy to gather more information about the human body and health, while engineers designed new techniques to grind grain using water mills.
The ancient Romans also invented a number of innovative methods to mine precious metals such as silver and gold.
But even with all these accomplishments, the ancient Romans are most often remembered as exceptional architects.
The early kings laid the foundation for a massive sewer system, and the leaders of the republic began the first aqueducts, some of which are still in use today.
Roman craftsmen and laborers also built many public buildings and temples.
The Romans' mastery of concrete technology, arch construction, and city planning left a legacy of impressive structures and urban features.
For instance, the town square, or forum, was a space purposefully left open to encourage meetings among citizens and provide a place for leaders to speak to their people.
Many modern cities, including Beijing, New York, and Moscow, have adopted this tradition and feature public squares in their downtown areas.
Wealthy aristocrats erected giant stone amphitheaters for gladiatorial games.
These sporting events were between professional fighters, and ended when one of the two competitors died at the hands of the other.
Sometimes men were even pitted against animals such as bears, tigers, and bulls; of course, the animals almost always won.
But the Romans' thirst for blood was great, and gladiatorial games attracted thousands of spectators; venues were often larger than modern soccer fields.
One of these, the Colosseum, which was built in 69 AD, was able to seat more than 45,000 people.
The ruins of this amphitheater still attract tourists in droves.
It's also interesting to note that the English word "colossal," meaning very big, gets its name from this impressive structure.
Surprisingly, evidence of Roman engineering can even be found as far away as England, which the Roman army occupied as a military outpost and called "Britannia."
The town of London was a central training ground for soldiers and a bustling hub of commerce.

One of the tasks of the Roman soldiers stationed in England was to build a wall across the country's northern boundary to prevent Scottish tribes from invading, as well as to mark the empire's frontier.
The remains of this barrier, named Hadrian's Wall after the reigning emperor at the time of its completion, still run across the northern part of England from the North Sea to the Irish Sea.
It was made a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987 and attracts about a million tourists each year.
The Romans also managed to build an extensive network of roads from Rome to its outlying territories, spanning more than 85,000 kilometers.
These paved pathways allowed legions to move swiftly from place to place, and provided easy trade routes for the many cities under the control of the empire.
Although they were quite simply constructed, these roads were instrumental in the rise of the Roman Empire and its ultimate dominance over the Mediterranean region for more than two thousand years.
At its pinnacle, the empire was so vast that it could truly be said that all roads led to Rome.

episodes.title: Frank Lloyd Wright: Agitator, Tester, and Wise Man

subtitle.text: Along the majestic Museum Mile in Manhattan, New York City, is one museum that visitors come to see
not just for the fine art inside, but for the building itself—the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, designed
by American architect Frank Lloyd Wright. The outside of the Guggenheim resembles a stack of ribbons. The round
building, finished in 1959, seamlessly weaves natural beauty with the sophisticated cityscape. Once visitors step into the cool
interior of the Guggenheim Museum, they follow a single path that winds in a continuous spiral through the
museum’s collection and special exhibits. The Guggenheim’s first curator, a German baroness named Hilla Rebay, said to
the architect, "I need a fighter, a lover of space, an agitator, a tester, and a wise man
. . . I want a temple of spirit, a monument!" The museum encompasses all those things and
proves its designer, Frank Lloyd Wright, to be one of the foremost architects of the modern age. On
June 8, 1867, Frank Lloyd Wright was born to a schoolteacher mother and preacher father in the
midwestern state of Wisconsin. When he was young, his mother gave him a set of Froebel building blocks,
which can be assembled in different ways. Wright later commented that those blocks influenced his approach to architecture;
the simple geometric forms in all his designs reflect this. As a child, Wright worked on his uncle’s
farm. Although he entered the University of Wisconsin at Madison in 1886, he never studied architecture because
there weren’t any courses available. He studied engineering until 1887, when he moved to Chicago to work as
an architectural apprentice—first under J. L. Silsbee, and then under Louis Sullivan. In 1893, Wright left Sullivan’s firm
and started his own. He began to design buildings that would be identified as the "prairie style,"
which stressed the importance of nature and of blending into the surrounding land. This style immediately began to
influence many other American architects and European designers. Wright, however, excelled at it. In order to appreciate the
significance of the prairie style, we must look at the Victorian houses that were the norm for residential
buildings at the turn of the twentieth century. Victorian houses, which were often three or four stories
high, were built to emphasize the vertical. They had many walls to support the beams and upper floors,
resulting in cramped, dark interiors. Furthermore, they had many distinct rooms, each with its own purpose and walled
off from the others. Prairie-style houses, on the other hand, emphasized the horizontal, reflecting the flat land of
the Midwest where Wright had grown up. They had low, sloping roofs and low chimneys to blend
in with the surrounding fields. They also featured long overhangs that elongated the living space. They were referred
to as "open plan" houses because they had few inner walls. As a result, the living area was
often one large, continuous room—light, airy, and spacious. This was a revolution in architecture, one that the public
embraced wholeheartedly. The Robie House, built in Chicago in 1910, is a famous example of the prairie
style, and many claim it started the revolution in modern architecture. Frank Lloyd Wright used a construction technique
known as the cantilevered beam to execute his bold design. A cantilevered beam is supported at only one
end, so it can extend into space without other walls to hold it up. This construction method allows
for an overhang without external support. The Robie House and other prairie homes used cantilevered beams to
do away with many of the supporting walls common in Victorian homes, making an open layout possible. In
Wright’s work, we see another facet of his architectural philosophy, which is that homes ought to blend smoothly
into their surroundings. Wright preached that our dwellings are a reinterpretation of nature, which led to their
being described as "organic architecture." As his mentor Louis Sullivan had stressed time and again, "Form follows function."
Wright, however, took that motto one step further, to "Form and function are one." This meant that he
respected the characteristics of the building materials and considered how the building would be used. Wright also looked
at the building site and its surroundings in order to design something that would harmonize with the
local environment. Many of Wright’s buildings show an ingenuity that was clearly before its time. The Imperial Hotel
in Japan, for example, was built with an innovative floating technique that Wright claimed would protect it against
earthquakes. That was indeed what happened; the Imperial Hotel was one of the few buildings left standing in
Tokyo after the Great Earthquake of 1923. Another classic example is Fallingwater, a family home built in
rural Pennsylvania in the 1930s and ’40s on top of an active waterfall. The home’s many windows and
balconies give people inside the building the feeling of being outside with nature. Its terraces of reinforced concrete
protrude from the main building much as boulders would, and the house melts into the scenery. The use
of natural construction materials—such as stone, which blends in with the forest and water—adds to the illusion
that the house had always been a part of the waterfall. The sound of water can even be
heard throughout the house. Throughout his career, Wright lectured, wrote, and published extensively. After the stock market crash
in 1929, when virtually all construction projects in the United States stopped, Wright spent a great deal
of time writing and lecturing about his architectural philosophy. In 1932, he wrote the first of his books
on urban problems, called The Disappearing City . It was during the Great Depression that he developed the
concept of Usonian houses, which were his version of affordable urban housing. Set on a concrete slab with
no attic and no basement, these houses were low cost, quickly constructed, and intended for families. They
were flat-roofed, usually one-story concrete buildings that were meant to provide housing for the growing urban population. Indeed,
many suburban houses today are built using the same basic principles. The enormous impact that Frank Lloyd Wright
has had on modern architecture cannot be overstated. In his personal life, he broke many barriers as well.
He was married three times, lived with other women while still married, and even ran away with
the wife of one of his clients! As a matter of fact, he lost many commissions because of
his scandalous lifestyle. Yet, as with his art, he believed in the "destruction of the box," or exploring
outside the barriers of conventional thinking. Frank Lloyd Wright died on April 9, 1959, just months before his
Guggenheim was complete. He never saw the finished museum, but its continued popularity proves that visitors appreciate
the risks Wright took. With this museum and many other designs, Wright certainly left his mark on architecture.

episodes.title: Beatlemania

subtitle.text: The noise of the crowd was tremendous as the four young lads from Liverpool, a port city in northwestern England, stepped out of their plane.
John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison, and Ringo Starr were all members of the radical new pop band the Beatles, and this was their first trip to the United States.
More than three thousand girls had lined up at Kennedy International Airport in New York City to greet the handsome quartet.
They were screaming, shouting, and crying with excitement.
Many held up signs with messages to the young men, such as "I love you, please stay!" and "Welcome to America." The frenzy was incredible.
Even the members of the band, who had toured all over Europe, felt overwhelmed by the reaction of the American fans.
It was February 7, 1964, a day that would change the face of popular culture forever.
By the time the Beatles arrived in America, they had already earned quite a reputation for themselves in Europe.
They were well-known musicians by 1962, when they signed a contract with a record label, EMI Records, and recorded at London's Abbey Road Studios for the first time.
Despite their popularity in Europe, the band was surprised at the extraordinary welcome they received in the United States and the success that would follow.
Their song "Love Me Do" had peaked at only number 17 on the British pop charts.
But the Beatles quickly put together a second single, "Please Please Me," and this time, the song reached number two in the United Kingdom.
When their first album, also titled [i@Please Please Me@i], was released in the UK in 1963, it was an instant hit, making the members of the band international celebrities.
It was obvious from the very beginning that the Beatles were not just an average pop band; they were charismatic, talented, and most importantly, willing to experiment with a rock-and-roll sound.
In 1960s Europe, many American rock-and-roll musicians had become quite popular, but the Beatles brought a unique quality to the genre.
Their tunes incorporated aspects of Celtic folk music, giving them a livelier, more rebellious flavor.
Even though the lyrics and melodies were quite simple, their songs spoke directly to the dreams and desires of their fans.
Teenage girls, in particular, were crazy about them, while young boys and audiophiles appreciated their musical skills.
Frenzied fans appeared whenever and wherever they performed. The media called this "Beatlemania."
The Beatles attracted the attention of Ed Sullivan, a famous American personality, who invited them to perform on his variety show on national television.
On February 10, their performance was broadcast into the living rooms of millions of viewers across the continent.

This was the first time that most North Americans had ever seen the British group and their distinctive sense of fashion: they wore black suits with ties and had collar-length, straight hair falling over their eyes and growing over their ears, a radical departure from the typical hairstyles of the day.
Within days, young men were requesting these "mop-top" haircuts from their barbers and wearing clothes that were similar in style to those of the band.
Meanwhile, "Please Please Me" was topping the charts, and their record company released a new version of their album for the American market.
On the cover, the Beatles wore black turtlenecks; days later, these also became hot items, as did the style of leather cap worn by John during their tour.
Companies even began selling Beatle wigs and costumes to eager customers. Anything and everything British was considered cool, hip, and desirable.
Not only did the Beatles revolutionize fashion in the United States, but they also changed the way that the general public appreciated music.
Fondness for the Beatles encouraged enthusiasts to explore other British musicians, such as the Rolling Stones and the Who.
Many journalists called the success of so many UK musicians the "British Invasion" and commented on the reversal of an earlier trend, when American groups had achieved stardom in the UK.
For two years, from 1964 to 1966, British musicians dominated global music charts.
The Beatles, however, decided that it was time to grow up and produce more mature and diverse albums.
They stopped touring in 1966 in order to focus on studio work.
George, who had learned to play the sitar, used the instrument on several songs.
Before long, everyone was interested in Indian music, and many young people were learning to play the sitar.
Some rock historians even credit the Beatles with starting the world music trend.
In 1967, the Beatles released [i@Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band@i], an album now widely accepted as one of the greatest albums ever recorded.
The album sold like hotcakes, but some critics were hesitant to embrace it, believing that the band had become too experimental and strayed too far from its roots.
Others heralded the album as a welcome transformation that signaled a step forward for the band.
The impact of the new style on the industry, however, was indisputable.
Unfortunately, conflict was erupting within the band: John and Paul had different opinions about the direction the Beatles should take.

Paul wanted his wife's father, the tycoon Lee Eastman, to take over the business affairs of the band; John was preoccupied with the creative side and was skeptical that Eastman could manage a musical group.
The disagreements intensified, and in 1970, Paul officially quit the band—the Beatles were splitting up.
This, however, was only the beginning of new chapters for the "Fab Four," as they were known.
George went on to record numerous solo albums and work on projects with other musicians. Ringo performed with a number of successful groups.
Paul played with a new band, Wings, until 1981, and released many solo albums in a variety of styles as well.
John and his wife, Yoko Ono, recorded several new albums together and became involved with the antiwar movement building in response to the Vietnam War.
One of John's songs, "Imagine," whose lyrics celebrate the possibility of a world at peace, is regarded by many as the most influential pop song of the twentieth century.
Sadly, John was shot and killed outside his New York apartment on December 8, 1980, by a crazed admirer.
Instead of a funeral, Yoko asked that all of his fans take ten minutes of silence to pause and remember their hero, his music, and the music of the Beatles.

The following Sunday, in a planned vigil, millions of people around the world, including thirty thousand in his hometown and one hundred thousand in New York, bowed their heads in silence to reflect on John Lennon and the Beatles.
With their sublime songs, unique style, and rare creativity, they had changed the world.
